analysis.one_liner: Gives drug makers six extra months of monopoly pricing when a drug wins approval for a rare-disease use.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a bipartisan pair of senators, was referred to a Senate committee in June 2017 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a drug company gets an already-approved drug approved for a new use treating a rare disease, this bill would extend the company's exclusive sales rights by six months — on top of other extensions it already has. It would also require a company seeking orphan-drug exclusivity for a drug already approved for the same disease to prove its version is meaningfully better, and it would let generic copies omit pediatric labeling that is protected by patent or exclusivity. The bill was introduced by Sen. Orrin Hatch with Sen. Robert Menendez, sent to the Senate health committee, and died there without ever being considered.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug makers gain the most: a guaranteed six-month extension of monopoly pricing each time one of their already-approved drugs wins approval for a rare-disease indication, which they can stack on top of pediatric and infectious-disease extensions. Companies could also keep developing repurposed drugs for small patient populations with the added revenue stream this creates. Generic drug makers get a narrower benefit, since they could be approved without carrying labeling for pediatric uses protected by someone else's patent or exclusivity.

how_it_helps.text: Grants an automatic six-month extension of marketing exclusivity whenever a drug or biologic is approved for a new indication that is a rare disease or condition, with the extension applying to the underlying exclusivity period [S2][S3].
Makes the six months additive: it is in addition to pediatric exclusivity and qualified-infectious-disease-product exclusivity, and each product can receive this extension only once [S2][S3].

Requires a sponsor seeking seven-year orphan-drug exclusivity for a drug that is the same as an already approved orphan drug for the same condition to demonstrate 'clinical superiority' — a significant therapeutic advantage in efficacy, safety, or patient care [S2][S3].

Expands to brand-name drugs the provision letting generic copies be approved without labeling for pediatric indications when those indications are protected by patent or exclusivity, which can smooth generic entry [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Patients, insurers, and government health programs would pay monopoly prices for an extra six months on any blockbuster drug that picks up a rare-disease indication — a cost spread across everyone who buys medicines, in exchange for new incentives aimed at small rare-disease populations.

drawbacks.text: The six-month extension is automatic and does not require the new rare-disease indication to be clinically superior to existing treatments, so a company can lengthen a monopoly on an already-approved blockbuster drug without offering patients anything better [S2][S3].
Extensions stack: the six months are in addition to pediatric and qualified-infectious-disease exclusivity, so total protection for a single drug can stretch well beyond six months [S3].

Because only products approved after enactment qualify and each product gets one extension, the incentive is narrow, while the monopoly-pricing cost falls on all payers, including public programs like Medicare and Medicaid.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that paying longer monopoly prices on top-selling drugs is an expensive way to encourage repurposing for rare diseases, and that the benefit flows to small patient populations while the cost is spread across everyone who buys medicines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is real but narrow: repurposing an existing drug for a rare disease is cheaper and faster than inventing a new one, and a guaranteed exclusivity bonus gives companies a reason to do it. But the bill's central mechanism — an automatic, stackable six-month monopoly extension that requires no clinical advantage over existing treatments — means the cost lands on every patient, insurer, and public program that buys the affected drugs, while the benefit goes to the drug maker and a small patient group. Weighing longer monopoly pricing on blockbuster medicines against uncertain repurposing gains, the cost falls on far more people than the benefit reaches, and the bill is designed so that the industry benefit is guaranteed while the public benefit is not.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was filed, and the committee never took it up before that Congress ended, so it never came to a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Sen. Hatch introduced the bill on June 29, 2017, for himself and Sen. Menendez, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate HELP Committee the same day [S1][S3][S5].
The bill attracted five cosponsors, three Democrats and two Republicans [S4].
No further action — no committee markup, no floor vote, no House companion action recorded in this bill's history — occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients, insurers, and taxpayers are better off in the narrow sense that the automatic six-month monopoly extensions were never enacted, so no already-approved drugs gained extra protected pricing. Drug makers lost a new revenue stream, and patients with rare diseases did not get the repurposing incentive its sponsors promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients and payers; drug makers lost a windfall

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed extending exclusivity for drugs approved for new rare-disease indications.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; co-introducer
for.what_they_did: Joined Hatch as the Democratic co-introducer of the bill.

for.name: Rare disease and pediatric cancer patient groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported the bill, arguing the exclusivity extension would push companies to develop existing drugs for rare diseases and childhood cancers.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a markup or vote, so the bill never advanced past referral.

against.name: Patients For Affordable Drugs
against.role: Patient advocacy group focused on drug prices
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, arguing its automatic exclusivity extensions would delay cheaper generic competition and raise drug costs.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — Hatch (R) introduced it with Menendez (D), and the five cosponsors split three Democrats and two Republicans — so it died in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill hands them a guaranteed, stackable six months of extra monopoly pricing each time an already-approved drug wins a new rare-disease indication, with no requirement that the new use outperform existing treatments. That gain comes directly out of what patients, insurers, and public programs pay while cheaper generics wait.

The pediatric-labeling provision would make it easier to approve generic copies that omit labeling for patent- or exclusivity-protected pediatric uses, but the six-month extensions would delay their market entry on affected drugs, pushing the benefit and the cost in opposite directions.

industries.industry: Companies developing repurposed drugs for rare diseases
industries.note: A guaranteed revenue bonus would lock repurposing-for-rare-diseases into the orphan-drug business model, which could speed development for small patient populations while tying it to extended monopoly pricing rather than to any requirement of clinical superiority.
